best_db_match.text: You are a senior officer working in the national drug regulatory authority. A highly reputable domestic pharmaceutical company has developed a new, low-cost drug for treating a rare, terminal type of pediatric cancer that kills thousands of poor children in India every year. The drug has shown extremely promising results in initial phases of clinical trials. However, during a routine compliance audit of the phase-III trial data, your team discovers that the company has committed serious procedural and ethical violations. They bypassed the strict informed consent protocols for several trial subjects from marginalized socio-economic backgrounds and suppressed data regarding mild-to-moderate long-term hepatic side effects in a small percentage of patients. The company management approaches you, admitting the procedural lapses but pleading for a cover-up or a conditional fast-track approval. They argue that stalling the drug's launch for a fresh round of trials will take at least three years, double the production cost, and result in the preventable deaths of thousands of poor children who cannot afford the highly expensive imported alternatives. (a) What are the ethical dilemmas and professional conflicts in this case? (b) As a regulatory officer, what decision would you take, and how would you justify it?
